title: Ὁ Νόστος τῶν Ἀτρεϊδῶν
titleEn: The Tale of Agamemnon's Murder — Odyssey 3.210–312
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Nestor wonders aloud whether Telemachus will ever be able to punish his mother's suitors, and Telemachus doubts that the gods favor him so openly. Athena, still disguised as Mentor, gently rebukes his despair, reminding him that death comes to all alike even under the gods' care. Telemachus then turns the talk from grief to knowledge, asking the long-lived Nestor to tell him exactly how Agamemnon died. Nestor tells the whole story: Aegisthus's seduction of Clytemnestra while Agamemnon was away at Troy, the murder of the returning king, and Orestes' revenge eight years later — alongside the separate, storm-driven voyage that scattered Menelaus's fleet on the way home. Nestor's speech is still running as this part ends, with Menelaus's arrival at the funeral feast for Aegisthus.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l: Him then answered the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor answered him:
sentences.n: This whole-line reply formula already stands in odyssey-010 (3.102) and is reused unchanged. Although the same line closed the previous part, the speech it opens here is a fresh one: Nestor is answering a new question Telemachus has just put to him.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλ’, ἐπεὶ δὴ ταῦτά μ’ ἀνέμνησας καὶ ἔειπες,
φασὶ μνηστῆρας σῆς μητέρος εἵνεκα πολλοὺς
ἐν μεγάροις ἀέκητι σέθεν κακὰ μηχανάασθαι·
sentences.tr:
ō phil’, epei dē tauta m’ anemnēsas kai eeipes,
phasi mnēstēras sēs mēteros heineka pollous
en megarois aekēti sethen kaka mēchanaasthai·
sentences.i: “Friend, since you have reminded me of this and spoken of it, they say that many suitors are, for your mother's sake, contriving evil in the halls against your will;
sentences.n: ἔειπες keeps the augment ἐ- unfused with the verb's initial vowel (root Ϝειπ-), where Attic contracts the two into the diphthong of εἶπες; this is a separate phenomenon from the diectasis of a contract verb such as μηχανάασθαι below. σέθεν is the Homeric genitive of σύ (= σοῦ). μηχανάασθαι is uncontracted, for μηχανᾶσθαι (Attic), genuine diectasis as at 1.32.

sentences.t:
εἰπέ μοι, ἠὲ ἑκὼν ὑποδάμνασαι, ἦ σέ γε λαοὶ
ἐχθαίρουσ’ ἀνὰ δῆμον, ἐπισπόμενοι θεοῦ ὀμφῇ.
sentences.tr:
eipe moi, ēe hekōn hypodamnasai, ē se ge laoi
echthairous’ ana dēmon, epispomenoi theou omphēi.
sentences.l:
Tell me, whether willingly you submit, or whether you, at least, the people
hate throughout the land, following a god's voice.
sentences.i: Tell me whether you submit to this willingly, or whether the people hate you throughout the land, following some god's voice.
sentences.n: ὑποδάμνασαι is present passive, 2nd sg., of the athematic epic verb ὑποδάμνημι (a -νημι by-form of δαμάζω, ‘subdue’); its ending -ασαι is the primitive mediopassive ending added directly to the stem, not a contracted or uncontracted form of anything in Attic, which does not keep this conjugation. ὀμφή is a divine voice or oracular utterance, distinct from plain speech — the suggestion is that some prophecy has turned the people against Telemachus.

sentences.t:
τίς δ’ οἶδ’ εἴ κέ ποτέ σφι βίας ἀποτίσεται ἐλθών,
ἢ ὅ γε μοῦνος ἐὼν ἢ καὶ σύμπαντες Ἀχαιοί;
sentences.tr:
tis d’ oid’ ei ke pote sphi bias apotisetai elthōn,
ē ho ge mounos eōn ē kai sympantes Achaioi;
sentences.l:
Who knows whether, coming, he will someday pay them back for their violence,
whether he alone, or even all the Achaeans together?
sentences.i: Who knows whether he will come one day and pay them back for their violence, whether alone or with all the Achaeans together?
sentences.n: μοῦνος is Ionic for μόνος. κέ is the epic equivalent of ἄν, here with the future middle ἀποτίσεται in an open condition. βίας is accusative plural, ‘acts of violence’.

sentences.t:
εἰ γάρ σ’ ὣς ἐθέλοι φιλέειν γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
ὡς τότ’ Ὀδυσσῆος περικήδετο κυδαλίμοιο
δήμῳ ἔνι Τρώων, ὅθι πάσχομεν ἄλγε’ Ἀχαιοί—
οὐ γάρ πω ἴδον ὧδε θεοὺς ἀναφανδὰ φιλεῦντας,
sentences.tr:
ei gar s’ hōs etheloi phileein glaukōpis Athēnē,
hōs tot’ Odyssēos perikēdeto kydalimoio
dēmōi eni Trōōn, hothi paschomen alge’ Achaioi—
ou gar pō idon hōde theous anaphanda phileuntas,
sentences.l:
For if so gleaming-eyed Athena should wish to love you,
as then for glorious Odysseus she cared,
in the land of the Trojans, where we Achaeans suffered pains—
for never yet have I seen gods so openly loving,
sentences.i: For if gleaming-eyed Athena should choose to love you as she then cared for glorious Odysseus in the land of the Trojans, where we Achaeans suffered our pains — for I have never yet seen gods show such open love,
sentences.n: περικήδετο is an unaugmented imperfect (Attic περιεκήδετο); the augment is optional in Homer, and this is a genuine case of its absence. κυδαλίμοιο is a genitive in -οιο (= -ου). ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω (Attic εἶδον), the same pattern as the convention's own example ἴδεν. This long conditional sentence runs from 3.218 to 3.224; Murray marks a parenthetical aside at 3.221–222 with dashes, but since the whole sentence would otherwise run past four lines, the unit is cut here at the clearest comma rather than at Murray's dash.

sentences.t:
ὡς κείνῳ ἀναφανδὰ παρίστατο Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη—
εἴ σ’ οὕτως ἐθέλοι φιλέειν κήδοιτό τε θυμῷ,
τῶ κέν τις κείνων γε καὶ ἐκλελάθοιτο γάμοιο.
sentences.tr:
hōs keinōi anaphanda paristato Pallas Athēnē—
ei s’ houtōs etheloi phileein kēdoito te thymōi,
tō ken tis keinōn ge kai eklelathoito gamoio.
sentences.i: as Pallas Athena stood openly at that man’s side — if she were willing to love you and care for you in her heart the same way, then surely one of those men would forget his marriage.”
sentences.n: ἀναφανδά ‘openly’ is repeated from the previous unit for emphasis; this line closes the parenthetical aside begun at 3.221, resuming the εἰ-clause of 3.218 with the echoing εἴ σ’ οὕτως ἐθέλοι φιλέειν of 3.223. τῶ is ‘then, therefore’, correlative with the εἰ of 3.218 and 3.223. ἐκλελάθοιτο is a reduplicated aorist optative of ἐκλανθάνομαι, ‘forget utterly’; γάμοιο is a genitive in -οιο. This closes Nestor's opening speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This whole-line reply formula already stands in odyssey-004 (1.388 — odyssey-004 covers 1.325–443) and is reused unchanged. It is the fourth of the reply-formulas fixed in the conventions, used specifically for Telemachus.

sentences.t: ὦ γέρον, οὔ πω τοῦτο ἔπος τελέεσθαι ὀίω·
sentences.tr: ō geron, ou pō touto epos teleesthai oiō·
sentences.l: “Old man, not yet do I think this word will be fulfilled;
sentences.i: “Old man, I do not think this word will be fulfilled;
sentences.n: ὦ γέρον is the house-fixed address, used every time it recurs. τελέεσθαι is uncontracted (Attic τελεῖσθαι). ὀίω is the epic first-person ‘I think, suppose’ (= οἴομαι).

sentences.t: λίην γὰρ μέγα εἶπες·
sentences.tr: liēn gar mega eipes·
sentences.l: for too great a thing you have said;
sentences.i: for that is too much to hope for;
sentences.n: λίην is Ionic for λίαν ‘exceedingly’, as already at 1.46. εἶπες is the ordinary aorist of λέγω/φημί, here with the augment fused into the diphthong, unlike the unfused ἔειπες at 3.211.

sentences.t: ἄγη μ’ ἔχει.
sentences.tr: agē m’ echei.
sentences.l: Amazement holds me.
sentences.i: I am amazed at the thought.
sentences.n: ἄγη ‘amazement, wonder’ is a rare noun related to ἄγαμαι ‘marvel at’. The clipped, three-word sentence marks Telemachus's blunt disbelief before he explains himself in the next unit.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἂν ἐμοί γε
ἐλπομένῳ τὰ γένοιτ’, οὐδ’ εἰ θεοὶ ὣς ἐθέλοιεν.
sentences.tr:
ouk an emoi ge
elpomenōi ta genoit’, oud’ ei theoi hōs etheloien.
sentences.l:
Not for me, at least, hoping,
would these things happen, not even if the gods so willed it.”
sentences.i: Not even in my hopes could I believe it would happen, not even if the gods willed it so.”
sentences.n: ἐλπομένῳ is the present participle of ἔλπομαι ‘hope, expect’, dative agreeing with ἐμοί. γένοιτ(ο) and ἐθέλοιεν are both optatives of unfulfilled wish/condition. This closes Telemachus's brief, doubtful reply.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe thea, glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: This line already stands in odyssey-002 (1.178 — odyssey-002 covers 1.96–212, not Book 2) and is reused unchanged. The narrator names her plainly as the goddess, though Telemachus still knows her only as Mentor, the old family friend.

sentences.t: Τηλέμαχε, ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων.
sentences.tr: Tēlemache, poion se epos phygen herkos odontōn.
sentences.l: “Telemachus, what a word has escaped you, the fence of your teeth.
sentences.i: “Telemachus, what a word is this that has got past the fence of your teeth!
sentences.n: φύγεν is unaugmented (Attic ἔφυγεν), governing two accusatives σε and ἕρκος ὀδόντων, the same idiom as the fixed formula at 1.64. This line is metrically irregular as transmitted: scanned by hand, the naturally short second syllable of Τηλέμαχε has to stand long to open the second foot, a genuine metrical lengthening at the head of the line.

sentences.t: ῥεῖα θεός γ’ ἐθέλων καὶ τηλόθεν ἄνδρα σαώσαι.
sentences.tr: rheia theos g’ ethelōn kai tēlothen andra saōsai.
sentences.l: Easily could a god, if willing, even from afar save a man.
sentences.i: A god, if willing, could easily save a man even from far away.
sentences.n: σαώσαι is a potential aorist optative without κε/ἄν, a construction that occurs occasionally in Homer. τηλόθεν carries the directional suffix -θεν, ‘from afar’.

sentences.t:
βουλοίμην δ’ ἂν ἐγώ γε καὶ ἄλγεα πολλὰ μογήσας
οἴκαδέ τ’ ἐλθέμεναι καὶ νόστιμον ἦμαρ ἰδέσθαι,
ἢ ἐλθὼν ἀπολέσθαι ἐφέστιος, ὡς Ἀγαμέμνων
ὤλεθ’ ὑπ’ Αἰγίσθοιο δόλῳ καὶ ἧς ἀλόχοιο.
sentences.tr:
bouloimēn d’ an egō ge kai algea polla mogēsas
oikade t’ elthemenai kai nostimon ēmar idesthai,
ē elthōn apolesthai ephestios, hōs Agamemnōn
ōleth’ hyp’ Aigisthoio dolōi kai hēs alochoio.
sentences.l:
I myself would wish, having suffered many pains,
to come home and see the homecoming day,
rather than, having come, to perish at my own hearth, as Agamemnon
perished, by the guile of Aegisthus and his own wife.
sentences.i: For my part I would wish, after suffering many pains, to come home and see the day of my homecoming, rather than come home only to die at my own hearth, as Agamemnon died by the guile of Aegisthus and his own wife.
sentences.n: ἐλθέμεναι is an infinitive in -έμεναι. νόστιμον ἦμαρ is the house-fixed formula. ἧς is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν, ‘his own’, easily mistaken for the relative. ἐφέστιος means ‘at one's own hearth’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι θάνατον μὲν ὁμοίιον οὐδὲ θεοί περ
καὶ φίλῳ ἀνδρὶ δύνανται ἀλαλκέμεν, ὁππότε κεν δὴ
μοῖρ’ ὀλοὴ καθέλῃσι τανηλεγέος θανάτοιο.
sentences.tr:
all’ ē toi thanaton men homoiion oude theoi per
kai philōi andri dynantai alalkemen, hoppote ken dē
moir’ oloē kathelēisi tanēlegeos thanatoio.
sentences.l:
But death, indeed, the same for all, not even the gods
can ward off, even from a dear man, whenever indeed
the deadly fate takes down of death that lays-at-length.”
sentences.i: But indeed death, the common lot, not even the gods themselves can ward off from a man they love, whenever the deadly fate of death that lays men at length shall take him down.”
sentences.n: The third line repeats verbatim the line already shipped at odyssey-005 (2.99 — odyssey-005 covers 2.1–102, not Book 5), and its wording is reused here; τανηλεγής, the epithet of θάνατος, is of unknown meaning (noted there). ἀλαλκέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν of the reduplicated aorist ‘ward off’. ὁμοίιον is ‘common to every man alike’. This closes Athena's speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This line already stands in odyssey-003 (1.213 — odyssey-003 covers 1.213–324, not Book 3) and is reused unchanged — the same reply-formula as 3.225, here with the feminine pronoun since Telemachus answers ‘Mentor’, whom the narrator has just called a goddess.

sentences.t: Μέντορ, μηκέτι ταῦτα λεγώμεθα κηδόμενοί περ·
sentences.tr: Mentor, mēketi tauta legōmetha kēdomenoi per·
sentences.l: “Mentor, no longer let us speak of these things, grieved though we are;
sentences.i: “Mentor, let us no longer speak of this, much as it grieves us;
sentences.n: λεγώμεθα is a hortatory subjunctive. κηδόμενοί περ uses περ with a participle for concessive force, ‘though grieving’, the same construction as ἱέμενός περ at 1.6. Telemachus still addresses the disguised goddess by the name of Odysseus's old companion Mentor.

sentences.t:
κείνῳ δ’ οὐκέτι νόστος ἐτήτυμος, ἀλλά οἱ ἤδη
φράσσαντ’ ἀθάνατοι θάνατον καὶ κῆρα μέλαιναν.
sentences.tr:
keinōi d’ ouketi nostos etētymos, alla hoi ēdē
phrassant’ athanatoi thanaton kai kēra melainan.
sentences.l:
For that man there is no longer a true homecoming,
but for him already the immortals have devised death and black doom.
sentences.i: There is no longer any real homecoming for him; the immortal gods have already ordained death for him, and black doom.
sentences.n: ἐτήτυμος ‘true, real’ echoes ἀτρεκέως-type language used elsewhere for reliable report. φράσσαντ(ο) is an unaugmented aorist middle of φράζω ‘devise, contrive’. κήρ is doom or death's agent, personified and regularly ‘black’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐθέλω ἔπος ἄλλο μεταλλῆσαι καὶ ἐρέσθαι
Νέστορ’, ἐπεὶ περὶ οἶδε δίκας ἠδὲ φρόνιν ἄλλων·
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ ethelō epos allo metallēsai kai eresthai
Nestor’, epei peri oide dikas ēde phronin allōn·
sentences.l:
But now I wish to inquire after another matter, and to ask
Nestor, since beyond others he knows judgments and wisdom;
sentences.i: But now I want to ask about something else, and to question Nestor, since he knows more than others about what is right and wise;
sentences.n: περὶ … οἶδε is the periphrasis ‘to know beyond, surpassingly’, governing the genitive ἄλλων, the same construction as περὶ … νόον ἐστὶ βροτῶν at 1.66. δίκη here is ‘judgment, right custom’, not yet the abstract ‘justice’.

sentences.t: τρὶς γὰρ δή μίν φασιν ἀνάξασθαι γένε’ ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.tr: tris gar dē min phasin anaxasthai gene’ andrōn·
sentences.l: for three times, they say, he has ruled over generations of men;
sentences.i: for they say he has ruled over three generations of men;
sentences.n: ἀνάξασθαι, the aorist middle infinitive of ἀνάσσω (elsewhere usually + dative), here takes the accusative γένε(α) ‘generations’ as its direct object, with the genitive ἀνδρῶν ‘of men’ depending on γένεα, not on the verb. This is the poem's own account of Nestor's proverbial longevity, spanning three generations.

sentences.t: ὥς τέ μοι ἀθάνατος ἰνδάλλεται εἰσοράασθαι.
sentences.tr: hōs te moi athanatos indalletai eisoraasthai.
sentences.l: so that to me immortal he seems to look upon.
sentences.i: so that to look at him he seems immortal to me.
sentences.n: τε here is the epic τε that marks a general, standing impression, not a mere connective. εἰσοράασθαι is uncontracted (Attic εἰσορᾶσθαι), diectasis as at 1.32; ἰνδάλλεται is ‘appears, seems’.

sentences.t: ὦ Νέστορ Νηληϊάδη, σὺ δ’ ἀληθὲς ἐνίσπες·
sentences.tr: ō Nestor Nēlēïadē, sy d’ alēthes enispes·
sentences.l: O Nestor, son of Neleus, but you speak the truth:
sentences.i: Nestor, son of Neleus — tell me the truth:
sentences.n: This is not the whole-line vocative already fixed at 3.79 (which continues μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν); only the opening ὦ Νέστορ Νηληϊάδη is shared, and that address is kept consistent. ἐνίσπες is the aorist imperative of ἐνέπω/ἐνίσπω ‘tell, declare’ (cf. ἔννεπε, 1.1); ἀληθές, ‘true(ly)’, is a distinct word from the fixed ἀτρεκέως-formula and is translated on its own terms.

sentences.t: πῶς ἔθαν’ Ἀτρεΐδης εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων;
sentences.tr: pōs ethan’ Atreïdēs eury kreiōn Agamemnōn;
sentences.l: How did he die, Atreus' son, wide-ruling Agamemnon?
sentences.i: How did Agamemnon, Atreus' son and wide-ruling lord, die?
sentences.n: ἔθαν(ε) is the ordinary aorist of θνῄσκω ‘die’ (root θαν-); Homer also has an unaugmented θάνε beside it, so the form is not itself remarkable. εὐρὺ κρείων ‘ruling widely’ is a title of kings with broad domains.

sentences.t: ποῦ Μενέλαος ἔην;
sentences.tr: pou Menelaos eēn;
sentences.l: Where was Menelaus?
sentences.i: Where was Menelaus at the time?
sentences.n: ἔην is the epic imperfect of εἰμί (= ἦν).

sentences.t:
τίνα δ’ αὐτῷ μήσατ’ ὄλεθρον
Αἴγισθος δολόμητις, ἐπεὶ κτάνε πολλὸν ἀρείω;
sentences.tr:
tina d’ autōi mēsat’ olethron
Aigisthos dolomētis, epei ktane pollon areiō;
sentences.l:
and what destruction did he contrive against him,
Aegisthus of guileful counsel, when he killed a man far better?
sentences.i: and what death did Aegisthus of guileful counsel contrive for him, when he killed a man far better than himself?
sentences.n: μήσατ(ο) is an unaugmented aorist middle of μήδομαι ‘devise, contrive’ (Attic ἐμήσατο); compare the augmented form of the same verb at 3.303. Αἴγισθος δολόμητις is the house-fixed epithet, kept distinct from the table's ‘blameless Aegisthus’.

sentences.t:
ἦ οὐκ Ἄργεος ἦεν Ἀχαιικοῦ, ἀλλά πῃ ἄλλῃ
πλάζετ’ ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους, ὁ δὲ θαρσήσας κατέπεφνε;
sentences.tr:
ē ouk Argeos ēen Achaiikou, alla pēi allēi
plazet’ ep’ anthrōpous, ho de tharsēsas katepephne;
sentences.l:
Was he not in Achaean Argos, but wandering
somewhere else among men, and he, taking courage, killed him?”
sentences.i: Was Agamemnon not in Achaean Argos, but wandering elsewhere among men, so that Aegisthus took courage and killed him?”
sentences.n: πλάζετ(ο) is unaugmented (Attic ἐπλάζετο), from πλάζω ‘drive astray, wander’, the passive of the same verb that opened the poem (1.2, 1.75). κατέπεφνε does carry the augment (κατ-έ-πεφν-ε), in addition to the reduplication πε- built into the aorist stem of the defective verb πέφνω ‘slay’ (cf. the unaugmented by-form πέφνον); the two features are separate and both present here. This closes Telemachus's second speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l: Him then answered the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor answered him:
sentences.n: The same whole-line formula as 3.210, reused unchanged; it opens Nestor's long tale of Agamemnon's death, which is not finished within this part.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, τέκνον, ἀληθέα πάντ’ ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.tr: toigar egō toi, teknon, alēthea pant’ agoreusō.
sentences.l: “Well then, I will tell you, child, all the truth.
sentences.i: “Well then, my child, I will tell you the whole truth.
sentences.n: τοιγάρ ‘well then, therefore’ introduces a considered answer. τέκνον, ‘child’, is Nestor's affectionate address to Telemachus. ἀληθέα, neuter plural, is cognate with ἀληθές at 3.247.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι μὲν τάδε καὐτὸς ὀίεαι, ὥς κεν ἐτύχθη,
εἰ ζωόν γ’ Αἴγισθον ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἔτετμεν
Ἀτρεΐδης Τροίηθεν ἰών, ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.tr:
ē toi men tade kautos oieai, hōs ken etychthē,
ei zōon g’ Aigisthon eni megaroisin etetmen
Atreïdēs Troiēthen iōn, xanthos Menelaos·
sentences.i: You can well imagine for yourself how it would have turned out if fair-haired Menelaus, the son of Atreus, coming home from Troy, had found Aegisthus alive in the halls;
sentences.n: ὀίεαι is the second-person present of ὀίομαι ‘think, suppose’ (cf. ὀίω, 3.226). ἐτύχθη is the aorist passive of τεύχω, ‘came to pass’. Τροίηθεν carries the ablatival suffix -θεν. ξανθὸς Μενέλαος is the house-fixed epithet.

sentences.t:
τῶ κέ οἱ οὐδὲ θανόντι χυτὴν ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἔχευαν,
ἀλλ’ ἄρα τόν γε κύνες τε καὶ οἰωνοὶ κατέδαψαν
κείμενον ἐν πεδίῳ ἑκὰς ἄστεος, οὐδέ κέ τίς μιν
κλαῦσεν Ἀχαιιάδων·
sentences.tr:
tō ke hoi oude thanonti chytēn epi gaian echeuan,
all’ ara ton ge kynes te kai oiōnoi katedapsan
keimenon en pediōi hekas asteos, oude ke tis min
klausen Achaiiadōn·
sentences.l:
then not even for him, dead, would they have heaped up a mound of earth,
but dogs and birds of prey would have torn him apart,
lying in the plain far from the city, nor would any
of the Achaean women have wept for him;
sentences.i: then not even in death would they have heaped earth over him, but dogs and birds would have torn him apart as he lay in the plain far from the city, and none of the Achaean women would have wept for him;
sentences.n: χυτὴν ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἔχευαν, ‘they would have poured a heaped mound of earth’, is the standard image of burial. κατέδαψαν is the aorist of δάπτω ‘tear, devour’. Ἀχαιιάδων is the same form as the fixed Ἀχαιϊάδες, ‘the Achaean women’.

sentences.t: μάλα γὰρ μέγα μήσατο ἔργον.
sentences.tr: mala gar mega mēsato ergon.
sentences.l: for a very great deed he had contrived.
sentences.i: for he had done a monstrous thing.
sentences.n: μήσατο is again the unaugmented aorist middle of μήδομαι, the same verb as at 3.249 above, contrasting with the augmented ἐμήσατο at 3.303 — Homer freely uses both forms of one verb.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς μὲν γὰρ κεῖθι πολέας τελέοντες ἀέθλους
ἥμεθ’·
sentences.tr:
hēmeis men gar keithi poleas teleontes aethlous
hēmeth’·
sentences.l:
For we there, many trials accomplishing,
were staying;
sentences.i: For we were there, sitting through many hard trials,
sentences.n: ἥμεθ(α) is the imperfect middle of ἧμαι ‘sit, remain’. ἀέθλους is uncontracted (Attic ἄθλους, cf. 1.18); τελέοντες is likewise uncontracted, ‘accomplishing’.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ εὔκηλος μυχῷ Ἄργεος ἱπποβότοιο
πόλλ’ Ἀγαμεμνονέην ἄλοχον θέλγεσκ’ ἐπέεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ eukēlos mychōi Argeos hippobotoio
poll’ Agamemnoneēn alochon thelgesk’ epeessin.
sentences.l:
but he, at ease, in a corner of horse-pasturing Argos,
again and again beguiled Agamemnon's wife with his words.
sentences.i: while he, at his ease, in a corner of Argos where horses graze, was working again and again on Agamemnon's wife with his words.
sentences.n: θέλγεσκ(ε) is an iterative imperfect in -σκε, ‘kept beguiling’; iteratives of this type never take the augment, so its absence here is not a case of the ordinary optional Homeric augment. ἱπποβότοιο is a genitive in -οιο. ἐπέεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἦ τοι τὸ πρὶν μὲν ἀναίνετο ἔργον ἀεικὲς
δῖα Κλυταιμνήστρη· φρεσὶ γὰρ κέχρητ’ ἀγαθῇσι·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ē toi to prin men anaineto ergon aeikes
dia Klytaimnēstrē· phresi gar kechrēt’ agathēisi·
sentences.l:
But she, indeed, at first refused the unseemly deed,
heavenly Clytemnestra; for she was possessed of a good mind;
sentences.i: Now she, indeed, at first refused the shameful deed, heavenly Clytemnestra, for she had a good understanding;
sentences.n: ἀναίνετο is a genuinely unaugmented imperfect (Attic ἠναίνετο). δῖα, kept as ‘heavenly’ throughout this edition (cf. δῖα θεάων, δῖος of Odysseus), here modifies Clytemnestra directly — an ironic touch given what follows. κέχρητ(ο), perfect middle of χράομαι + dative, is ‘was furnished with’.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔην καὶ ἀοιδὸς ἀνήρ, ᾧ πόλλ’ ἐπέτελλεν
Ἀτρεΐδης Τροίηνδε κιὼν εἴρυσθαι ἄκοιτιν.
sentences.tr:
par d’ ar’ eēn kai aoidos anēr, hōi poll’ epetellen
Atreïdēs Troiēnde kiōn eirysthai akoitin.
sentences.l:
And beside her there was also a minstrel man, to whom many commands
the son of Atreus gave, going to Troy, to guard his wife.
sentences.i: And there was a minstrel beside her too, whom the son of Atreus, when he set out for Troy, charged strictly to watch over his wife.
sentences.n: πὰρ … ἔην is tmesis for πάρειμι, ‘was beside’. Τροίηνδε carries the directional suffix -δε. εἴρυσθαι, present infinitive of εἴρυμαι/ἐρύομαι ‘guard, protect’, shares its root with ἐρρύσατο at 1.6.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή μιν μοῖρα θεῶν ἐπέδησε δαμῆναι,
δὴ τότε τὸν μὲν ἀοιδὸν ἄγων ἐς νῆσον ἐρήμην
κάλλιπεν οἰωνοῖσιν ἕλωρ καὶ κύρμα γενέσθαι,
τὴν δ’ ἐθέλων ἐθέλουσαν ἀνήγαγεν ὅνδε δόμονδε.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē min moira theōn epedēse damēnai,
dē tote ton men aoidon agōn es nēson erēmēn
kallipen oiōnoisin helōr kai kyrma genesthai,
tēn d’ ethelōn ethelousan anēgagen honde domonde.
sentences.l:
But when the fate of the gods bound him to be overcome,
then indeed, leading the minstrel to a desert island,
he left him to become the prey and spoil of birds,
and her, willing, willing herself, he led up to his own house.
sentences.i: But when the fate of the gods bound him to be brought low, Aegisthus led the minstrel away to a desert island and left him there to become the prey and spoil of birds, and led the woman away, willing as she was, to his own house.
sentences.n: δαμῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of δαμάζω, ‘be overcome’ (of death or fate). κάλλιπεν = κατέλιπεν, syncopated. ἐθέλων ἐθέλουσαν, the same verb repeated for subject and object, stresses her complicity. ὅνδε δόμονδε doubles the directional suffix -δε, ‘to his own home’.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ μηρί’ ἔκηε θεῶν ἱεροῖς ἐπὶ βωμοῖς,
πολλὰ δ’ ἀγάλματ’ ἀνῆψεν, ὑφάσματά τε χρυσόν τε,
ἐκτελέσας μέγα ἔργον, ὃ οὔ ποτε ἔλπετο θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
polla de mēri’ ekēe theōn hierois epi bōmois,
polla d’ agalmat’ anēpsen, hyphasmata te chryson te,
ektelesas mega ergon, ho ou pote elpeto thymōi.
sentences.l:
And many thigh-pieces he burned on the sacred altars of the gods,
and many offerings he hung up, both woven cloths and gold,
having accomplished a great deed, which never he had hoped in his heart.
sentences.i: And he burned many thigh-pieces on the gods' sacred altars, and hung up many offerings, cloths and gold, now that he had brought off a great deed he had never hoped in his heart to achieve.
sentences.n: ἔκηε is the Homeric aorist of καίω ‘burn’ (beside Attic ἔκαυσα), with the root vowel lengthened rather than a plain sigmatic aorist. μηρία, the thigh-bones wrapped in fat, are the portion burned for the gods in sacrifice. ἀγάλματα are votive offerings, literally ‘things that delight’.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς μὲν γὰρ ἅμα πλέομεν Τροίηθεν ἰόντες,
Ἀτρεΐδης καὶ ἐγώ, φίλα εἰδότες ἀλλήλοισιν·
sentences.tr:
hēmeis men gar hama pleomen Troiēthen iontes,
Atreïdēs kai egō, phila eidotes allēloisin·
sentences.l:
For we were sailing together, coming from Troy,
the son of Atreus and I, of one mind, friendly toward each other;
sentences.i: For we were sailing home together from Troy, the son of Atreus and I, on good terms with one another;
sentences.n: φίλα εἰδότες ἀλλήλοισιν, literally ‘knowing friendly things to each other’, is an idiom for being on trusting terms — a contrast, as Nestor now turns to his own and Menelaus's voyage, with the treachery just described in Mycenae.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε Σούνιον ἱρὸν ἀφικόμεθ’, ἄκρον Ἀθηνέων,
ἔνθα κυβερνήτην Μενελάου Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων
οἷς ἀγανοῖς βελέεσσιν ἐποιχόμενος κατέπεφνε,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote Sounion hiron aphikometh’, akron Athēneōn,
entha kybernētēn Menelaou Phoibos Apollōn
hois aganois beleessin epoichomenos katepephne,
sentences.l:
But when we reached sacred Sounion, the headland of Athens,
there the helmsman of Menelaus did Phoebus Apollo,
with his gentle shafts assailing, slay,
sentences.i: But when we reached sacred Sounion, the headland of Athens, there Phoebus Apollo came upon Menelaus's helmsman with his gentle arrows and killed him,
sentences.n: ἀφικόμεθ(α) is the aorist middle of ἀφικνέομαι ‘arrive, reach’. Σούνιον, ἄκρον Ἀθηνέων is Cape Sounion at the tip of Attica. ἀγανοῖς βελέεσσιν, ‘gentle shafts’, is Homer's regular way of describing a swift, painless death sent by a god. The whole 278–283 sentence runs six lines and is cut here, at its clearest syntactic pause, rather than carried past the four-line limit.

sentences.t:
πηδάλιον μετὰ χερσὶ θεούσης νηὸς ἔχοντα,
Φρόντιν Ὀνητορίδην, ὃς ἐκαίνυτο φῦλ’ ἀνθρώπων
νῆα κυβερνῆσαι, ὁπότε σπέρχοιεν ἄελλαι.
sentences.tr:
pēdalion meta chersi theousēs nēos echonta,
Phrontin Onētoridēn, hos ekainyto phyl’ anthrōpōn
nēa kybernēsai, hopote sperchoien aellai.
sentences.l:
holding the steering-oar in his hands, of the running ship,
Phrontis, son of Onetor, who surpassed the tribes of men
in piloting a ship, whenever storm-blasts drove on.
sentences.i: as he held the steering-oar of the racing ship in his hands — Phrontis, son of Onetor, who surpassed all men living at piloting a ship whenever storms bore down.
sentences.n: ἐκαίνυτο is the imperfect of καίνυμαι ‘surpass, excel’ with the genitive φῦλ(α) ἀνθρώπων. κυβερνῆσαι is an epexegetic aorist infinitive, ‘at piloting’. σπέρχοιεν is a general/iterative optative with ὁπότε. Phrontis is a minor named victim, singled out by patronymic in the epic manner.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὁ μὲν ἔνθα κατέσχετ’, ἐπειγόμενός περ ὁδοῖο,
ὄφρ’ ἕταρον θάπτοι καὶ ἐπὶ κτέρεα κτερίσειεν.
sentences.tr:
hōs ho men entha kateschet’, epeigomenos per hodoio,
ophr’ hetaron thaptoi kai epi kterea kteriseien.
sentences.l:
So there he was held back, eager though he was to press on his way,
so that he might bury his companion and render him funeral rites.
sentences.i: So Menelaus was held there, eager as he was to press on his journey, so that he might bury his companion and pay him funeral honours.
sentences.n: κατέσχετ(ο) is the ordinary aorist middle of κατέχω, ‘was held back, detained’ (aorist stem σχ-, the same stem as ἔσχον). ἐπειγόμενός περ repeats the concessive περ-with-participle pattern seen at 3.240. κτερίσειεν is from κτερίζω, ‘render funeral honours’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ καὶ κεῖνος ἰὼν ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον
ἐν νηυσὶ γλαφυρῇσι Μαλειάων ὄρος αἰπὺ
ἷξε θέων,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē kai keinos iōn epi oinopa ponton
en nēusi glaphyrēisi Maleiaōn oros aipy
hixe theōn,
sentences.l:
But when he too, going upon the wine-faced open-sea,
in hollow ships, the steep mountain of Malea
reached, speeding on,
sentences.i: But when he too, as he sailed over the sea that has the look of wine in his hollow ships, came running to the steep headland of Malea,
sentences.n: οἴνοπα πόντον is the house-fixed formula. This sentence (3.286–290) runs five lines and is cut here, at the comma after θέων where the syntax pauses most, rather than past the four-line limit. θέων is the present participle of θέω ‘run, speed’.

sentences.t:
τότε δὴ στυγερὴν ὁδὸν εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
ἐφράσατο, λιγέων δ’ ἀνέμων ἐπ’ ἀυτμένα χεῦε,
κύματά τε τροφέοντο πελώρια, ἶσα ὄρεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
tote dē stygerēn hodon euryopa Zeus
ephrasato, ligeōn d’ anemōn ep’ aytmena cheue,
kymata te tropheonto pelōria, isa oressin.
sentences.l:
then indeed a hateful path did far-thundering Zeus
devise, and of the shrill winds a blast poured out,
and waves were reared up, monstrous, like mountains.
sentences.i: then far-thundering Zeus planned a hateful course for them, and poured down a blast of shrill winds, and huge waves rose up like mountains.
sentences.n: εὐρύοπα Ζεύς is the house-fixed epithet. ἐπ(ὶ) … χεῦε is tmesis for ἐπέχευε, ‘poured upon’. τροφέοντο is an uncontracted imperfect passive of τρέφω in its rarer sense ‘thicken, swell’ (of waves). ἶσα ὄρεσσιν, ‘equal to mountains’, gives the waves' size.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα διατμήξας τὰς μὲν Κρήτῃ ἐπέλασσεν,
ἧχι Κύδωνες ἔναιον Ἰαρδάνου ἀμφὶ ῥέεθρα.
sentences.tr:
entha diatmēxas tas men Krētēi epelassen,
hēchi Kydōnes enaion Iardanou amphi rheethra.
sentences.l:
There, having split the fleet apart, some he drove to Crete,
where the Cydonians dwelt around the streams of the Iardanus.
sentences.i: There he split the fleet apart, and drove some of the ships to Crete, where the Cydonians lived around the streams of the Iardanus.
sentences.n: διατμήξας is the aorist participle of διατμήγω ‘cut apart, split’; ἐπέλασσεν is the aorist of πελάζω ‘bring near, drive to’. The Cydonians are a people of western Crete; the river Iardanus is otherwise unattested outside epic.

sentences.t:
ἔστι δέ τις λισσὴ αἰπεῖά τε εἰς ἅλα πέτρη
ἐσχατιῇ Γόρτυνος ἐν ἠεροειδέι πόντῳ·
sentences.tr:
esti de tis lissē aipeia te eis hala petrē
eschatiēi Gortynos en ēeroeidei pontōi·
sentences.l:
There is a certain smooth rock and steep, into the sea,
at the border of Gortyn, in the misty-looking sea;
sentences.i: There is a smooth rock, steep toward the sea, at the edge of Gortyn's land, in the misty-looking sea;
sentences.n: λισσή is ‘smooth, sheer’; αἰπεῖα is the feminine of αἰπύς, as in αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον (1.11). Gortyn is a city of Crete. ἠεροειδέι πόντῳ keeps the house-fixed rendering ‘the misty-looking sea’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα Νότος μέγα κῦμα ποτὶ σκαιὸν ῥίον ὠθεῖ,
ἐς Φαιστόν, μικρὸς δὲ λίθος μέγα κῦμ’ ἀποέργει.
sentences.tr:
entha Notos mega kyma poti skaion rhion ōthei,
es Phaiston, mikros de lithos mega kym’ apoergei.
sentences.l:
There the South Wind drives a great wave against the left-hand headland,
toward Phaestus, and a small rock keeps off the great wave.
sentences.i: There the South Wind drives a great wave against the headland on the left, toward Phaestus, and a small rock holds the great wave off.
sentences.n: Νότος, the South Wind, is personified. σκαιόν is ‘on the left’, from a sailor's viewpoint approaching from the west. Phaestus is a city of Crete. ἀποέργει is uncontracted (Attic ἀπείργει), ‘wards off’.

sentences.t:
αἱ μὲν ἄρ’ ἔνθ’ ἦλθον, σπουδῇ δ’ ἤλυξαν ὄλεθρον
ἄνδρες, ἀτὰρ νῆάς γε ποτὶ σπιλάδεσσιν ἔαξαν
κύματ’·
sentences.tr:
hai men ar’ enth’ ēlthon, spoudēi d’ ēlyxan olethron
andres, atar nēas ge poti spiladessin eaxan
kymat’·
sentences.i: The ships came in there, and the men barely escaped destruction, but the waves smashed the vessels against the reefs;
sentences.n: ἤλυξαν is the aorist of ἀλύσκω ‘escape, avoid’; σπουδῇ is ‘with effort, barely’. ἔαξαν, aorist of ἄγνυμι ‘break, shatter’, has its subject κύματα held over to the next line for emphasis. σπιλάδεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ τὰς πέντε νέας κυανοπρῳρείους
Αἰγύπτῳ ἐπέλασσε φέρων ἄνεμός τε καὶ ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr:
atar tas pente neas kyanoprōireious
Aigyptōi epelasse pherōn anemos te kai hydōr.
sentences.l:
but the five dark-prowed ships,
to Egypt did the wind and the current carry and drive.
sentences.i: but the other five dark-prowed ships were carried by wind and current to Egypt.
sentences.n: κυανοπρῳρείους, ‘dark-prowed’, is built on κύανος, the dark-blue enamel used to decorate a ship's prow; the epithet recurs of ships generally and is recorded as a new house rendering. ἐπέλασσε is the same verb as at 3.291, with ἄνεμός τε καὶ ὕδωρ, ‘wind and current’, as its subject.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὁ μὲν ἔνθα πολὺν βίοτον καὶ χρυσὸν ἀγείρων
ἠλᾶτο ξὺν νηυσὶ κατ’ ἀλλοθρόους ἀνθρώπους·
sentences.tr:
hōs ho men entha polyn bioton kai chryson ageirōn
ēlato xyn nēusi kat’ allothroous anthrōpous·
sentences.l:
So he there, much livelihood and gold gathering,
wandered with his ships among men of another tongue;
sentences.i: So Menelaus wandered there with his ships among men of another tongue, gathering great store of livelihood and gold;
sentences.n: ἠλᾶτο is the imperfect middle of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’ (the initial α lengthens to η under the augment, then contracts). ἀλλόθροοι ἄνθρωποι is the house-fixed formula. βίοτος is ‘livelihood, means of life’, distinct from βίος ‘life’.

sentences.t: τόφρα δὲ ταῦτ’ Αἴγισθος ἐμήσατο οἴκοθι λυγρά.
sentences.tr: tophra de taut’ Aigisthos emēsato oikothi lygra.
sentences.l: Meanwhile these grievous things Aegisthus contrived at home.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Aegisthus was plotting these grievous things at home.
sentences.n: τόφρα ‘meanwhile’ correlates with the ὄφρα-type clauses tracing Menelaus's wanderings; the narrative now cuts back to events in Greece. ἐμήσατο, the augmented counterpart of μήσατ(ο) at 3.249 and 3.261, is the same verb shown both with and without the augment. οἴκοθι carries the locative suffix -θι. λυγρά is the house-fixed rendering ‘grievous’.

sentences.t:
ἑπτάετες δ’ ἤνασσε πολυχρύσοιο Μυκήνης,
κτείνας Ἀτρεΐδην, δέδμητο δὲ λαὸς ὑπ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr:
heptaetes d’ ēnasse polychrysoio Mykēnēs,
kteinas Atreïdēn, dedmēto de laos hyp’ autōi.
sentences.l:
and for seven years he ruled over Mycenae rich in gold,
having killed the son of Atreus, and the people were held subject beneath him.
sentences.i: For seven years he ruled over Mycenae rich in gold, after killing the son of Atreus, and the people were subject to him.
sentences.n: This unit's t follows the packet's print order exactly: Murray transposes 3.304 and 3.305, printing the line now numbered 305 before the line numbered 304, and this edition preserves that same order. ἤνασσε is the aorist of ἀνάσσω ‘rule over’ + genitive. πολύχρυσος ‘rich in gold’ is a stock epithet of wealthy Mycenae, recorded as a new house rendering. δέδμητο is a reduplicated pluperfect passive of δάμνημι, not an augmented form.

sentences.t:
τῷ δέ οἱ ὀγδοάτῳ κακὸν ἤλυθε δῖος Ὀρέστης
ἂψ ἀπ’ Ἀθηνάων, κατὰ δ’ ἔκτανε πατροφονῆα,
Αἴγισθον δολόμητιν, ὅ οἱ πατέρα κλυτὸν ἔκτα.
sentences.tr:
tōi de hoi ogdoatōi kakon ēlythe dios Orestēs
aps ap’ Athēnaōn, kata d’ ektane patrophonēa,
Aigisthon dolomētin, ho hoi patera klyton ekta.
sentences.l:
But in the eighth year, to him came evil, heavenly Orestes,
back from Athens, and he killed down the father-slayer,
Aegisthus of guileful counsel, who had killed his famous father.
sentences.i: But in the eighth year evil came upon him: heavenly Orestes arrived back from Athens and killed the slayer of his father, Aegisthus of guileful counsel, who had killed his famous father.
sentences.n: The last line is identical to a line already shipped at odyssey-003 (there closing a question); its wording, ‘Aegisthus of guileful counsel, who had killed his famous father’, is reused, adapted here to a declarative sentence. ἤλυθε is an epic by-form of ἦλθε (aorist of ἔρχομαι), not itself an unaugmented alternative to it. κατὰ … ἔκτανε is tmesis for κατέκτανε.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὁ τὸν κτείνας δαίνυ τάφον Ἀργείοισιν
μητρός τε στυγερῆς καὶ ἀνάλκιδος Αἰγίσθοιο·
sentences.tr:
ē toi ho ton kteinas dainy taphon Argeioisin
mētros te stygerēs kai analkidos Aigisthoio·
sentences.l:
And indeed he, having killed him, gave a funeral feast to the Argives
for his hateful mother and for cowardly Aegisthus;
sentences.i: And having killed him, Orestes gave a funeral feast to the Argives for his hateful mother and for cowardly Aegisthus;
sentences.n: δαίνυ is the imperfect of δαίνυμι ‘give a feast’, here the funeral banquet following the two deaths. στυγερῆς ‘hateful’ and ἀνάλκιδος ‘without strength, cowardly’ are Nestor's own harsh judgments on Clytemnestra and Aegisthus. Ἀργείοισιν is a dative plural in -οισι.

sentences.t:
αὐτῆμαρ δέ οἱ ἦλθε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος
πολλὰ κτήματ’ ἄγων, ὅσα οἱ νέες ἄχθος ἄειραν.
sentences.tr:
autēmar de hoi ēlthe boēn agathos Menelaos
polla ktēmat’ agōn, hosa hoi nees achthos aeiran.
sentences.l:
And on that very day there came to him Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
bringing many possessions, as many as his ships bore as a burden.
sentences.i: And on that very day Menelaus, good at the war-cry, arrived, bringing great store of possessions, as much as his ships could carry as cargo.
sentences.n: βοὴν ἀγαθός, ‘good at the war-cry’, a stock heroic epithet here given to Menelaus, is recorded as a new house rendering. αὐτῆμαρ stresses the swiftness of the reunion. This is the last unit of the part; Nestor's speech, begun at 3.254, is not finished here — in the fuller poem it continues well past 3.312, and it is left open rather than closed, to be picked up in the next part.
